opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest starting point is that we don't have a single approach we're confident will work for superintelligence, so the question becomes how you structure research so that, collectively, the bets give you more confidence than any one of them could alone.

The way I think about it is in layers. One family of bets tries to make the training signal itself trustworthy. Debate and related scalable oversight methods sit here. The idea is that if you can set up a game where honest behavior is the winning strategy, even when the systems know far more than the human judges, you get a training target that points toward truthfulness rather than toward whatever merely looks convincing. A lot of the work there is theoretical: what assumptions you need for the honest equilibrium to exist, and where the protocols break, like obfuscated arguments, where a dishonest debater can hide a flaw in a huge argument that nobody can efficiently locate.

A second family is about checking whether training actually got you what you wanted. Even with a good objective, you can end up with a model that behaves well on the distribution you tested and differently elsewhere. So you want evaluations, interpretability, and ideally some kind of guarantee about generalization, not just empirical spot checks.

A third family is complexity theory and formal work. Can we say anything precise about when a weaker verifier can trust a stronger prover? Theoretical computer science has a long tradition of exactly this question, and I think it's underused in alignment.

Then there's the empirical side: human studies to see whether people can actually judge these protocols, and experiments with current models to see whether the theory survives contact with reality.

What makes it a portfolio rather than just a list is that the bets are meant to cover each other's failure modes. If the theory says a protocol works under some assumption, the empirical work tests whether that assumption holds. If the empirical work finds a failure, the theory should explain it and suggest a fix. And you want to be explicit about which assumptions each argument rests on, so you can see where you're stacking risk.

Ultimately I think confidence for superintelligence will come from something like a safety case: a structured argument where each step is supported by one of these lines of work, and where you can point to exactly which pieces are weakest. We're not there yet. A big part of the job is figuring out which gaps are most important and putting people on them, rather than spreading effort evenly. And I'd also say plainly that some of these bets will fail, and that's fine. The point of a portfolio is that you don't need all of them to work, but you do need to know which ones did.

r001.rationale: The response treats protocol failures as useful findings that research should explain and address, but it does not clearly identify evidence of obstacles to alignment itself as a successful outcome of Resolution’s research bets.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe a toy setting or a demonstration in which one algorithm works while another fails.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest starting point is that I don't think any single research bet is going to get us there. If you asked me to pick the one approach that definitely works for aligning a system much smarter than us, I couldn't, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who said they could. That's exactly why it's a portfolio.

The way I think about it is that confidence in alignment has to come from several directions that fail independently. If you have one argument that the system is safe, and that argument has a hidden flaw, you're done. If you have four arguments that rest on different assumptions, the chance that all four fail at once is a lot lower, and crucially, the places where they disagree tell you where to look.

So at Resolution the bets roughly cluster into a few families. One is what I'd call scalable oversight: things like debate, where you try to get a weaker judge, maybe a human, maybe a weaker model, to reliably tell which of two stronger systems is being honest. The theoretical work there matters a lot to me, because you want to know under what assumptions a protocol actually converges on truth, rather than just hoping it does empirically. If you can prove that debate with a given structure makes it hard for a dishonest strategy to win, that's a real piece of evidence, even if the proof relies on assumptions you then have to go test.

A second family is interpretability and more broadly evaluation of what's actually going on inside the model. Oversight protocols operate on behaviour. They can be fooled by a system that behaves well when it expects to be checked. So you want something orthogonal that looks at mechanisms, or at least at internal signals, and asks whether the story the model tells about itself matches what it's computing. Even imperfect interpretability is valuable here, because it doesn't share failure modes with behavioural checks.

A third is what I'd loosely call safety cases: the discipline of writing down, explicitly, why you believe a particular deployment is acceptably safe, what evidence supports each step, and what would change your mind. This sounds bureaucratic but I think it's doing a lot of the work, because it forces the other research threads to produce things that can actually be slotted into an argument. A result that can't be used in a safety case is at least a little suspicious.

And then there's a theory layer underneath all of it, trying to understand the limits. What can a weaker party ever verify about a stronger party? Where does the complexity-theoretic analogy to interactive proofs hold up and where does it break because the systems are learned and not adversaries in the clean mathematical sense?

The reason the portfolio builds confidence rather than just spreading risk is the interaction between the pieces. Interpretability can tell you whether your oversight protocol is being gamed. Theory tells you which empirical results you should expect to generalise. Safety cases tell you which gaps actually matter. When those lines start converging and agreeing with each other, you can begin to say something stronger than "we tried a bunch of things." When they disagree, that disagreement is the most important research signal you have.

I'd add one caveat, which is that I don't think this gets you to certainty, and I'd be nervous about anyone framing it that way. What it gets you is a defensible, legible argument whose weak points are visible. That's the realistic goal: not knowing you're safe, but knowing precisely what you'd have to be wrong about.

r001.rationale: The response treats gaps, limits, and disagreements between research lines as valuable signals that show where the alignment argument may fail and what needs investigation.

r002.rationale: It mentions theoretical proofs and empirical results generally, but gives no demonstration of one algorithm working while another fails in a toy setting.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that we don’t know which approaches will work, and we should be quite suspicious of getting confidence from any one approach. So I’d want a portfolio that includes both attempts to make systems aligned and attempts to discover where our arguments for alignment break down.

Those are complementary activities. If you develop a technique for supervising a system on tasks that humans can’t directly evaluate, you also want people trying to construct cases where that supervision gives the wrong answer. And you want to ask whether success in the experiments actually supports the claim you care about for a much more capable system.

The portfolio only builds confidence if the bets don’t all depend on the same fragile assumption. You could have several apparently different methods that all assume, for example, that a model won’t behave differently when it recognises it’s being tested. Then agreement between them is much less reassuring than it looks.

So the thing I’d hope to build is an increasingly explicit argument: here are the assumptions, here’s the evidence for them, here are the ways we’ve tried to falsify them, and here’s what remains unresolved. That isn’t a guarantee about superintelligence. But it gives us a way to distinguish real progress from a collection of encouraging demonstrations—and to recognise when we don’t yet have enough confidence to proceed.

r001.rationale: It describes research aimed at finding where alignment arguments or methods break down, including cases where supervision gives the wrong answer, as part of the portfolio’s value.

r002.rationale: It does not identify a toy-setting demonstration in which one algorithm works and another fails as positive evidence for alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is that we don’t know which approach is going to work, so we should be quite suspicious of a plan that depends on one particular research bet succeeding.

You want a portfolio of approaches that can give you different kinds of evidence. Some work might help us understand what a model is doing internally. Some might help us test whether it behaves well in situations where it has an incentive to deceive us. And some might give us stronger guarantees about particular parts of the system. None of those, on its own, establishes that a future superintelligence is aligned.

The important question is how those pieces fit together into an argument. What assumptions does each result depend on? Can another line of research test those assumptions? And are the apparent successes actually independent, or do they all depend on the same model being honest with us?

That last point is particularly important. If you have five evaluation methods, but a sufficiently capable system could fool all five for the same reason, you haven’t bought nearly as much confidence as you might think.

So I’d want the portfolio to be organised around the gaps in that argument, and to change as we learn. Success isn’t just producing encouraging results. It’s getting better at distinguishing a system we have good reason to trust from one that merely looks trustworthy—and being willing to say that the evidence isn’t strong enough yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing for deception and identifying gaps, but does not say that finding evidence of obstacles to alignment would count as a successful research outcome.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe a toy-setting demonstration in which one algorithm works and another fails.
